intro: Paderewski plays Chopin’s C♯ minor Waltz in a 1917 recording. He is a passionate defender of rubato, the freedom to stretch and quicken a phrase; Chopin’s score already asks the pianist to move between three different paces.

sections.label: A · Long notes and curling replies
sections.mNote: Tempo giusto above a bass note and two chords

sections.label: B · The quicker descending tune
sections.mNote: Più mosso sets the right hand running

sections.label: C · D♭ major, more slowly
sections.mNote: Più lento: a long melody with answering inner notes

sections.label: D · Quavers and the opening melody
sections.mNote: C♯ minor returns with the two earlier tunes

sections.label: E · The last Più mosso
sections.mNote: The descending tune carries the ending

cues.title: A melody in pairs
cues.text: The right hand begins in two voices. Their long notes hang over the bar line before a quick flourish answers. The left hand supplies a bass note and two chords in each bar. Tempo giusto is Chopin’s opening instruction.
cues.evidence: Waltz score, opening Tempo giusto; Knute Snortum engraving (2023), p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The enemy of the metronome
cues.text: In his 1909 essay, Paderewski calls rubato “this irreconcilable foe of the metronome”. He rejects the idea that every moment borrowed by slowing must be paid back by speeding up. For a solo pianist, he writes, “What is lost is lost.”
cues.evidence: Paderewski, ‘Tempo Rubato’, written for Henry T. Finck’s Success in Music and How It Is Won (1909), chapter 28, pp. 454–61. https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol4no1/paderewski-tempo-rubato/

cues.title: The refrain between the songs
cues.text: Chopin builds the waltz around the running Più mosso tune. It appears three times: after the opening melody, after the D♭ major song and once more at the end. The quick descent is the familiar face between the longer conversations.
cues.evidence: The score’s complete sequence is Tempo giusto, Più mosso, Più lento, Più mosso, Tempo primo, Più mosso. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Six quavers against three beats
cues.text: The final Più mosso puts six running quavers above the left hand’s three beats. The melody falls in slurred arcs, then climbs high to begin again. Its last descent brings the piano home to C♯ minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
